items.title: RMIT builds dolphin-shaped minibot to skim oil spills

featured_image.name: Sneaker-sized 'Electronic Dolphin' robot could transform oil ...

items.description: Engineers at RMIT University in Australia have built a remote-controlled minibot shaped like a dolphin that skims oil from the surface of water using a filter inspired by the spiny structure of sea urchins. The proof-of-concept device, called the "Electronic Dolphin," is about the size of a sneaker and could offer a safer, more targeted way to respond to oil spills in sensitive environments.[1][2]

items.title: CSIRO and India complete world-first green steel trial using rice husk waste

featured_image.name: Australia-India partnership takes step closer to green steel ...

items.description:
Researchers from Australia and India have completed what they describe as a world-first commercial trial using agricultural waste to partially replace coal in steelmaking, offering a scalable pathway to cut emissions in one of the planet's most carbon-intensive industries.

The trial, announced on March 10 by CSIRO, Australia's national science agency, saw scientists blend rice husk pellets into gasifiers at a Jindal Steel facility in Odisha, India. Working alongside the Indian Institute of Science and RESCONS Solutions, a steel technology company incubated at IISc, the team substituted 5 and 10 percent of coal with locally sourced rice husk pellets while maintaining steady syngas production and no loss in operating performance.[1][2]

items.title: Scientists identify landing sites for China's first crewed moon mission

featured_image.name: China reveals how it plans to put astronauts on the moon by ...

items.description:
Chinese and international scientists have identified four potential landing sites in the volcanic Rimae Bode region on the moon's near side, advancing planning for what would be China's first crewed lunar mission before the end of the decade.

The findings, published March 9 in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Astronomy, present a detailed geological assessment of the equatorial region, which researchers describe as a "geological museum" combining high scientific value with safe conditions for astronaut access.[1][2]

items.title: UCL scientists reconstruct videos from mouse brain activity

featured_image.name: A new AI tool that can decode brain signals proves '95% accurate' on mice

items.description: Scientists at University College London have reconstructed 10-second video clips purely from the brain activity of mice, marking what researchers say is the first time natural movies have been successfully recovered from single-cell recordings in the visual cortex. The findings, published Monday in the journal eLife, could open new paths for understanding how the brain processes and distorts visual information.[1][2]

The milestone means that about one in every four iPhones produced worldwide is now made in India, as the company accelerates efforts to diversify manufacturing away from China amid persistent U.S. tariff pressures.[1]

items.title: ALMA detects high methanol levels in interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS

featured_image.name: An interstellar comet packed with alcohol? What ALMA found in 3I/ATLAS

items.description:
Astronomers using one of the world's most powerful radio telescope arrays have discovered that the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS contains extraordinary levels of methanol compared with hydrogen cyanide, a chemical fingerprint unlike nearly anything observed in comets born in our own solar system. The findings, announced by the ALMA Observatory on March 8, suggest the comet formed under conditions vastly different from those that shaped familiar solar system objects.[1]

The research team, led by Nathan Roth, a professor at American University, used ALMA's Atacama Compact Array in Chile to observe 3I/ATLAS multiple times in late 2025 as it drew closer to the Sun. On two separate observation dates, they measured methanol-to-hydrogen cyanide ratios of roughly 70 and 120, placing the comet among the most methanol-rich ever studied.[2][1]

"Observing 3I/ATLAS is like taking a fingerprint from another solar system," Roth said. "The details reveal what it's made of, and it's bursting with methanol in a way we just don't usually see in comets in our own solar system."[1]

items.title: Engineers hide data in heat radiation using 'negative light'

featured_image.name: New 'negative light' technology hides data transfers in ...

items.description: Engineers at UNSW Sydney and Monash University have built a communication system that conceals data transmissions within natural heat radiation, making them virtually undetectable. The technology, described in a paper published March 4 in the Nature Publishing Group journal Light: Science and Applications, exploits a phenomenon called "negative luminescence" to create what the researchers call "thermoradiative signatureless communication."[1][2]

items.title: Sydney researchers build AI chip that computes at speed of light

featured_image.name: Photonic chip that 'fits together like Lego' opens door to ...

items.description: Researchers at the University of Sydney have built a prototype artificial intelligence chip that processes data using light instead of electricity, performing calculations at the speed of light on a picosecond timescale — trillionths of a second. The nanophotonic chip, described in a study published in Nature Communications, points toward a future of faster and more energy-efficient AI hardware.[1][2]

items.title: Macron, IAEA chief open nuclear energy summit in Paris

featured_image.name: Macron to outline France's contribution to Europe's nuclear ...

items.description:
World leaders are convening in Paris on Monday for the second Nuclear Energy Summit, an event hosted by the French government in cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency to promote the expansion of civilian nuclear power at a moment of acute energy insecurity and escalating conflict in the Middle East.

French President Emmanuel Macron and IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi opened the summit, with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also delivering remarks. The gathering brings together heads of state and government, leaders of international organizations and financial institutions, and industry experts to discuss nuclear energy's role in decarbonization, energy security, and meeting surging electricity demand.[1][2][3][4]
